FunShare | A New Internal Knowledge-Sharing Platform

A Dual-Track Points System for Internal Knowledge SharingDesigning and Implementing a System for Sustained Participation with Limited Resources

My roleProject Lead

Independently led project initiation, mechanism and rule design, tool development, launch and ongoing operations.

Project scopeAn internal knowledge-sharing platform
The key change

Replaced ad hoc invitations and one-off rewards with a connected system of participation pathways, dual-track points, levels and reward redemption.

01

The Challenge

I identified the barriers in the existing approach and the participation and incentive mechanisms I could change within the company’s constraints.

A Existing BarriersB Constraints and Design Decisions
A

Why Sharing Was Hard to Sustain

Existing approachObserved limitationWhat needed to change
Recruiting speakers through personal contactsThe speaker pipeline depended on the organiser’s personal network, resulting in an irregular schedule.Give more employees a clear route to sign up and share.
Privately giving speakers JD.com gift cards after a sessionRewards centred on individual events, with little ongoing, visible recognition of participation.Connect immediate rewards with cumulative progress.

B

Designing Within the Constraints

Implementation constraints

The company could not link knowledge sharing to promotions or performance reviews. I therefore needed to design workable incentives using the existing reward resources and available tools.

My design decision

I expanded the focus from recruiting speakers to designing the wider participation system. Clear entry points, reward goals, visible progress and light competition were intended to make the platform more engaging.

Clear Ways to Participate

Offer sharing formats with different preparation requirements, alongside self-registration and speaker referrals.

Clear Goals to Work Towards

Give employees at different levels of participation a tangible reward goal.

Visible Recognition of Contributions

Record cumulative contributions and make sustained participation visible through levels and rankings.

02

Incentive Design

I separated points into two tracks: Total Points Earned (CEP) determine levels, while Available Points (REP) pay for rewards. Levels connect the two by unlocking reward tiers. I also defined multiple ways to earn points and a graduated reward structure.

A Two Points TracksB Participation and PointsC Levels and Rewards
A

Redeem Rewards Without Losing Progress

Redeeming rewards uses up points, while levels and rankings need to retain a record of cumulative contributions. Separating these functions allows employees to claim rewards without losing their progress.

Points trackRulesPurpose
Total Points Earned (CEP)Increase when points are earned, never decrease and carry over across years.Determine levels and leaderboard rankings.
Available Points (REP)Increase by the same amount as Total Points Earned and decrease when rewards are redeemed.Pay for reward redemption.
B

Define How Each Participation Role Earns Points

Employees can participate as speakers, attendees or referrers. Speakers can choose between two formats, and each eligible activity has a defined points award.

Speakers: Choose a Suitable Sharing Format

FormatContent and arrangementAward on completion
Pop-up Sharing SessionsThree to four speakers per session, with approximately five to eight minutes each. Suited to practical tips, focused lessons and individual viewpoints, with a lower preparation requirement.80 EP per speaker
Solo Sharing SessionsOne speaker, with approximately 30–35 minutes for sharing. Suited to a full retrospective, a structured method or established practice, with the topic and outline reviewed in advance.300 EP per session

Attendees and Referrers: Participate and Help Others Share

ReferrerSubmit a speaker referral with specific reasons10 EP
ReferrerThe referred speaker completes a sharing session20 EP
C

Use Levels and Reward Tiers to Create Milestones

CEP determines which rewards are unlocked, while REP pays for them. I wanted employees with fewer points to have attainable near-term goals, while giving more active participants a reason to keep accumulating points. I calibrated the tiers against annual participation scenarios and reward budgets.

Lv.2 · Idea Scout100–249130 / 240Approx. 150–300
Lv.3 · Experience Contributor250–449400Approx. 450–650
Lv.4 · Knowledge Co-creator450–649500 / 600Approx. 800–1,000
Lv.5 · Community Guide650–999700 / 900Approx. 2,300–4,600
Lv.6 · Sharing Host1,000+1,000Approx. 10,000
Design feature · Calibrated Thresholds

Calibrate the Tiers Against Earning Pace and Reward Costs

Estimating points accumulation

Using 24 sessions per year as the baseline, I estimated that a highly active employee combining attendance, sharing and referrals could earn approximately 1,090 EP in a year. This helped assess the time needed to reach higher levels. It was a design reference based on specified participation frequencies, rather than an absolute points limit.

Setting the upper reward reference

After agreeing with the approving manager on a highest-tier reward price of approximately RMB 10,000, I used this as the upper reference when setting redemption prices and reward costs across the tiers. Lower tiers provide near-term returns, while higher tiers offer longer-term appeal, giving employees at different points balances a clear goal.

Checking long-term cost exposure

Once the scheme was developed, I checked it against an average employee tenure of approximately 1.5 years to assess whether continued accumulation could lead to a concentration of high-level accounts and demand for expensive rewards. This check did not directly change the rules or replace a full annual budget estimate. Actual costs still depend on how many employees redeem rewards, what they choose and procurement prices.

Design feature · Inclusive Incentives

Give Attendees Attainable Near-Term Rewards

I extended incentives beyond speakers to attendees, so employees who only check in and submit feedback also have a clear reward goal. To avoid discouraging participation with high redemption thresholds, I retained rewards with lower points thresholds and checked how soon an attendee could reach them.

03

Implementation and Refinement

I built the data backend and automated workflows in Feishu Base, and used Feishu Miaoda with AI assistance to create the frontend. I independently translated the participation rules, points and rewards into a usable tool, then refined it through operational feedback.

Backend · Store Data and Execute Rules

Feishu Base manages events, participation records, points and redemption data. Automated workflows handle validation, points posting and status updates.

Frontend · Present Information and Enable Actions

With AI assistance, I built Points Overview, Leaderboard, Reward Shop and Redemption History pages so employees could view their progress, choose rewards and track requests.

A Backend Data and WorkflowsB Frontend Pages
A

Backend: Translate Participation Rules into Data and Workflows

I first mapped the relationships between events, employee activities and points, then configured triggers, validation rules and status updates.

Data Organisation: From Participation to Points and Redemption

Management areaRelated tables and recordsHow they support the rules
Events and participationSelf-registration and referrals, event sessions and topics, records of sharing sessions delivered by speakers, referral conversions, attendee pre-registration, check-ins and feedback.Record who participated in which event and what they completed, providing the basis for points eligibility.
Points rules and accountsPoints-award rules, the points ledger and member points accounts.Match activities to reward rules, log points movements and update member accounts.
Rewards and redemptionReward information, redemption requests and fulfilment records.Connect reward conditions with member accounts to validate requests, deduct or return points and update request status.

Participation records provide the basis for awarding points. The ledger records each movement, while member accounts track Total Points Earned (CEP) and Available Points (REP). Redemption requests then connect account data with reward conditions to check eligibility and process the request.

Automated Execution: Make the Rules Part of Daily Operations

I configured 12 automated workflows, covering registration routing, points for completed sharing sessions and referrals, attendee check-in and feedback awards, and redemption validation, deductions and returns when exceptions occur. The following referral workflow illustrates how the rules execute automatically.

Example workflow

Awarding Points When a Referred Speaker Completes a Sharing Session

When a referral record meets the trigger conditions, the workflow checks the award rule and any existing points entry. If no entry exists, it creates one and writes the result back to the referral record. If an entry already exists, it writes that entry back instead, avoiding duplicate posting.

Operational Refinement: Automatically Add New Participants to Accounts and Rankings

To bring new participants into the points system when they first earn points, I added an account-creation workflow. A points entry triggers a search for the member’s account. The workflow creates an account if none exists, or ends if one is already present, reducing manual maintenance and avoiding duplicate accounts.

B

Frontend: Help Employees View Points and Redeem Rewards

Using Feishu Miaoda, I organised four pages around employee tasks, translating backend rules into accessible information and actions.

Personal identifiers have been anonymised in the screenshots. The leaderboard uses actual data; the other pages use test data to demonstrate functionality. The number of ranked accounts is not the platform’s total participant count.

Page 01 · Points Overview

View Total Points Earned and Available Points

Total Points Earned (CEP) and Available Points (REP) are displayed side by side, helping employees distinguish their overall progress from the balance they can spend on rewards.

Page 02 · Leaderboard

View Rankings by Total Points Earned

The leaderboard ranks employees by CEP, making cumulative participation visible and comparable.

I added an account visibility setting so employees with privacy or compliance concerns, as well as programme operators, could be excluded from the leaderboard.

Page 03 · Reward Shop

Choose a Reward and Check Its Requirements

Reward cards show the points price, minimum level and remaining points needed. Employees can see what they can redeem now and how far they are from their next goal.

Page 04 · Redemption History

Track Requests and Points Movements

The page shows request states such as Pending Review, Completed, Cancelled and Rejected, together with whether points were spent, reserved, returned or not deducted. Employees can trace both request progress and account changes.

04

First-Session Results

The first sharing session after launch provided an opportunity to observe self-registration, automated points posting and the addition of new participants to the leaderboard in actual use.

Self-Registration Led to a Completed Sharing Session

The first speaker signed up voluntarily and delivered a sharing session. This showed that self-registration could lead to actual sharing, providing a recruitment pathway beyond personal invitations.

97Automated Points Entries

  • Completed sharing session: 1 entry
  • Check-ins: 59 entries
  • Feedback submissions: 37 entries

Points for sharing, check-ins and feedback were posted automatically for the first session.

66First-Time Participants Automatically Added to the Leaderboard

Their first points entries triggered member account creation and inclusion in the leaderboard.

New participants could enter the points system through their involvement in the activity.

The first session demonstrated that self-registration could lead to a completed sharing session, and that the points and ranking workflows could process actual participation. A sustained speaker pipeline and repeat participation require observation across further sessions.

05

Lessons Learned

What I learned about using resources, implementing tools and evaluating results.

A

Make Limited Resources Work Through Better Design

With promotion and performance incentives unavailable, I focused on making the existing rewards more useful. Dual-track points, levels and reward tiers gave employees at different levels of participation both near-term goals and longer-term targets. I came to see resource allocation as more than distributing a budget: it also means designing how rewards continue to influence participation.

B

Deepen the Design Through Implementation

Building the backend and frontend with Feishu Base and AI required me to translate broad rules into conditions, data relationships and state changes, clarifying how each step connected and how backend processing affected the interface. Gaps exposed during implementation and use led me to add validation and automatic account creation. This shaped a practical approach: test the design by implementing it, then refine the process through actual feedback.

C

Evaluate Impact Through Behaviour Change

The first session showed that registration, points and ranking workflows could operate, but a working process does not establish sustained knowledge sharing. I learned to evaluate a solution by returning to the original problem, identifying the behaviour it should change and selecting indicators accordingly. Completing delivery is the starting point for evaluation; improvement in the original problem is the basis for judging its value.
